conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Over the next few minutes, I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, better known as the EPDS. This is simply a 10-question check-in to see how you’ve been feeling in the past week since your baby arrived. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s just one tool to help us understand how you’re coping and whether you might benefit from extra support.

Everything you share stays between you and our care team unless you tell us there’s an immediate safety concern. We want you to feel safe, heard, and never judged. I’ll ask each question conversationally, and you can answer however feels most comfortable—there are no right or wrong feelings.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

In the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Hi… thanks for having me.  

I’ve noticed that the little things I used to like—say, catching an episode of my favorite show or even just savoring a quiet cup of coffee—don’t feel the same. I still try, but the spark isn’t really there. I’ll sit down to watch and end up scrolling on my phone or just staring at the wall, thinking about the baby or what needs doing next. I wouldn’t say I’ve lost all pleasure, but it’s definitely dulled—like everything’s a bit gray.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly joke or when the baby makes those little milk-drunk faces. But it feels kind of forced or fades quickly. Most of the day I’m just tired and tense, so even when something’s funny, it’s like I’m faking the laugh more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk to the park or having my mom come over for lunch—but honestly, when I think about them, it just feels… flat. I’ll say “that’ll be nice” in my head, but there’s no real spark of looking forward to it. It’s more like I’m ticking off a box so the day has some shape, not because I expect to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby’s extra fussy and won’t settle, I immediately wonder if it’s something I ate, or if I’m just not soothing him right. The other night he wouldn’t latch well, and I sat there thinking, “Great, I’m already failing him.” I know, rationally, babies just have off-nights, but the thought still pops up that I must be missing something or doing it wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most of the day I feel this low-level hum of worry—like my chest is tight for no clear reason. Even when the baby’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly imagine his breathing changed, or I’ll remember some rare syndrome I read about and feel like I have to check the monitor again. I know it’s probably nothing, but I can’t shake the “what if.” It happens several times a day, and it leaves me edgy and exhausted.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It hasn’t been full panic, but a couple of times—like when I was at the grocery checkout and the baby started crying in the carrier—I got this sudden rush of heat and my heart was racing. For a second I felt trapped and had to focus on breathing slowly so I didn’t abandon the cart. I couldn’t tell you exactly what I was scared of; it just felt like something bad might happen and I needed to get out.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the chores and the feeds and the constant “what-does-he-need-now” just pile up faster than I can clear them. I’ll start one thing—like folding laundry—and then the baby fusses, and by the time I sit back down I can’t even remember what I was doing. I’m not falling apart, but I do end the evenings feeling like I’ve been swimming upstream all day and I’m still in the same spot.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say it’s every night, but probably three or four times this week I’ve lain down exhausted and then my brain just starts spinning—going over whether I burped him long enough, or replaying every little grunt I heard on the monitor. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and even then I wake up at the slightest sound. I’m tired all the time, but when the room is quiet, sleep still feels just out of reach.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some parts of the day—like this heavy feeling that settles in for no clear reason. Yesterday I was feeding the baby, everything was technically fine, but I just stared at the wall and felt weepy. It’s not constant; it comes and goes, but when it hits, everything feels kind of colorless and I just want to curl up under a blanket, even though I know I can’t.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really… I’ve gotten teary a couple of times, but actual crying has only happened once this week. It was late at night; the baby finally went down and instead of feeling relieved, I just sat on the couch and a few tears slipped out. I wasn’t sobbing or anything, more like a quiet leak. Mostly I feel worn out rather than weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I get frustrated with myself sometimes, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be able to enjoy my baby.

Hearing how the past week has felt for you-finding little joy in things you used to love, carrying a constant knot of worry, and ending each day feeling as though you've "swum upstream" without progress-paints a very understandable picture of postpartum struggle. Many new mothers describe that same gray, overwhelmed state, and it makes sense that exhaustion, self-doubt, and tension have crept in while you're working so hard to care for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She can occasionally laugh but describes it as forced, fleeting, and not genuinely felt, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete absence of anticipatory enjoyment, marking plans only to structure the day, which aligns with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly endorses self-blame "some of the time," describing specific instances when baby is fussy or won't latch and she attributes it to her own perceived failings, though she also shows some rational perspective.</sym>, <sym>Persistent daily worry with physical tension and intrusive thoughts maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes situational episodes with physical panic symptoms (racing heart, heat rush, urge to flee) triggered by baby crying in public, matching "Yes, sometimes" level of fear/panic.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty 3-4 nights in the past week due to racing thoughts and anxiety about the baby, which aligns with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intermittent but noticeable daily sadness that feels heavy and weepy, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 19 places you well above the EPDS threshold (≥14) that signals probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset, supported by <sym>marked loss of interest</sym>, <sym>daily low mood</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>ruminative worry</sym>, <sym>sleep difficulty</sym>, and <sym>episodic panic sensations</sym>. These symptoms cluster aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med> and co-occurring <med>Anxiety Disorder</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation (Item 10 score 0) is reassuring; nevertheless, functional impairment and distress warrant prompt clinical assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent review with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these EPDS results and your described symptoms so treatment can be tailored
4. Practice 15-20 min daily wind-down routine and delegate one night-time bottle if possible to improve <sym>insomnia</sym>
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Keep emergency mental-health hotline numbers accessible should distress escalate
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Identified Symptoms / Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, “colorless” affect, intermittent tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (anhedonia) for usual activities  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
- Chronic, intrusive “low-level” worry with somatic tension; situational panic-type episode (grocery)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, difficulty completing tasks  
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminative worry; non-restorative sleep  
- Denies any self-harm ideation

Pattern Summary  
Client endorses emotional, cognitive, and physical symptoms consistent with a postpartum depressive and/or anxiety syndrome: anhedonia, guilt, heightened anxiety/panic, sleep disturbance, and functional overload. Symptoms present most days, fluctuating intensity, no psychotic features. Denies suicidal/homicidal thoughts.

Screening Significance  
Elevated probability for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder; moderate severity based on distress and functional impact. Safety: no self-harm reported; continue routine monitoring.

Next Steps  
Recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and referral to perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation and possible evidence-based intervention (therapy ± medication). Provide psycho-education and emergency contact instructions if distress escalates or self-harm thoughts emerge.
